lead.t: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is the most common parasitic infection worldwide, especially among children.

sets.t: Enterobius vermicularis and Ascaris lumbricoides — Essay Questions

snip.t: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is the most common parasitic infection worldwide, especially among children.
Transmission: Likely fecal-oral, possibly through eggs of *Enterobius vermicularis*.

qs.q: Which anatomical region serves as the primary habitat for adult Enterobius vermicularis worms?
o: Terminal ileum and rectum near the distal colon
Caecum, appendix, and ascending colon of the large intestine
Stomach and pyloric antrum of the upper gastrointestinal tract
Duodenum and proximal jejunum of the small intestine
qs.e: Adult pinworms reside in the caecum, appendix, and ascending colon. The duodenum is instead the hatching site for ingested eggs.

qs.q: Which clinical manifestation is uniquely associated with female genitourinary involvement in heavy Enterobius vermicularis infections?
o: Bilateral hydronephrosis and acute renal failure
qs.e: Female worms can aberrantly migrate into the vulva and vagina, causing vulvovaginitis and mucoid discharge. Painful vesicular lesions are typically viral in origin rather than parasitic.

qs.q: What defines the unique phenomenon of retroinfection in the life cycle of Enterobius vermicularis?
o: Ingested eggs bypass the intestine and hatch inside the bloodstream
Male worms re-enter the appendix after mating
Adult worms travel backward from the rectum into the stomach
Larvae hatch on perianal skin and migrate back into the colon
qs.e: Retroinfection occurs when eggs hatch directly on the perianal skin, and the resulting larvae migrate back through the anus into the colon. Autoinfection, by contrast, involves hand-to-mouth transfer after scratching.

qs.q: Which specific bodily location serves as the primary habitat for adult Enterobius vermicularis worms?
qs.e: Adult pinworms inhabit the cecum, appendix, and adjacent portions of the ascending colon. They do not primarily reside in the upper small intestine like Ascaris.

qs.q: An 8-year-old child with perianal itching is evaluated for a pinworm infection. What is the primary infective form of Enterobius vermicularis ingested during transmission?
qs.e: Transmission occurs via the ingestion of embryonated eggs containing larvae through contaminated fingers, fomites, or food. Unfertilized eggs are not the infective stage.

qs.q: Which mechanism describes how Enterobius vermicularis can maintain a persistent infection without new external exposure?
qs.e: Retroinfection occurs when eggs hatch on the perianal skin, and larvae migrate back into the colon. This is unique to pinworms and contributes to high persistence.

qs.q: A physician suspects Enterobius vermicularis in a school-aged child but orders a perianal tape test instead of a stool ova and parasite exam. Why are standard fecal smears generally ineffective?
qs.e: Eggs are rarely found in feces because gravid females migrate to the perianal region at night to deposit them. Perianal swabs are therefore required for diagnosis.

qs.q: A 7-year-old child is diagnosed with Enterobius vermicularis, and the pediatrician advises treating all household members simultaneously. What is the main reason for this strategy?
qs.e: High recurrence rates due to autoinfection mean that treatment should include all household members to completely clear the infection source. Sharing utensils is not the primary transmission mode.
